name: Chloe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential; I’d like to hear what you’d say publicly and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Chloe Farah, twenty-seven, and I lead carpenters on building sites. I rent a small place by myself and have a few months of expenses saved. I learned the trade from my aunt’s joinery shop, though this is the first time I’ve been responsible for a whole crew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like for you? What do you enjoy and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I mark up the drawing before the crew arrives, then check the delivery and assign the cuts. I like when the apprentices ask why we are doing something instead of just copying my hands. I get tired from correcting late changes that nobody told the site crew about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a tool that catches a missing hinge on the list might save us a trip. I’d still ask the crew to check the pieces against the opening before anyone makes a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t think a small change will remove much of my site work. I have a few months saved and some nearby builders I know, so I could get through a short gap if one contract ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d test the list checker against the order for a set of kitchen cabinets. I’d keep leading the crew and add to my savings when the contractor pays on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because the tool would be helping with a check, not taking the whole job. I’m still careful with my savings because building work can pause between contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare the checker’s result against?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare every cabinet width to the room plan and to the measurements we took on site. A box count can be right while the dimensions are wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it found a mistake that the paper list missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show the foreman the mismatch and ask him to approve the corrected order. I’d use it again after that, but I’d want somebody responsible to check each change.

say: I’d try a checker that catches a **missing hinge**.
I still compare every piece with the **site opening** before a cut.
think: I don’t expect this small change to remove much of **my site work**.
I can manage a brief pause with **a few months saved**.
do: Test the list checker against a **cabinet order**.
Keep leading the crew and add to savings after **payday**.
feel: I feel **calm** because the tool helps with one check.
S0.quote: A box count can be right while the dimensions are wrong.
fieldNote: Chloe accepts a tool for one task but insists on **site measurements**.
Her savings and local contacts make a brief pause **manageable**, but she still watches contracts closely.

steps.text: Test the list checker against a cabinet order
Keep leading the carpentry crew on site
Add to savings after contractor pay arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a schedule tool could help if it shares late changes with the people actually on site. I don’t want the office to assume that a task is finished because a box was checked on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do some scheduling and notes as crew lead, and that part might change. I’m not quick to trust a new system, but I can learn it if I see how it handles an actual site delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the foreman to show me the new scheduler on a job with a clear delivery plan. I’d keep the cabinet and framing work moving and ask early if my hours were changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about my scheduling tasks changing, but I have a few months saved and local contacts. I can learn after I see a practical reason for the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check that it handles a delay properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d put in a late delivery and see whether the next trades get notified. If the electrician is still waiting for our wall, the schedule must show that instead of pretending the job is on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this scenario say that AI causes fewer construction projects to start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can’t say that from the card. I’d look at the contractor’s booked work and ask whether the crew roster changes before making a claim about fewer projects.

say: I’d use a schedule tool that shares **late changes** with the site crew.
I don’t treat a checked screen box as proof that **work is finished**.
think: I expect my scheduling and notes to **change**.
I can learn a system after seeing it handle a **real site delay**.
do: Ask the foreman to show the new scheduler on a clear **delivery job**.
Keep the **cabinet and framing work** moving.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with savings and local contacts if work shifts.
S1.quote: If the electrician is still waiting for our wall, the schedule must show that instead of pretending the job is on time.
fieldNote: Chloe asks for a **practical demonstration** before trusting changed schedules.
She rejects an unsupported claim that AI reduces starts and checks the contractor’s **booked work** with care.

steps.text: Learn the scheduler from the foreman on a clear delivery job
Keep cabinet and framing work moving on site
Wait for the contractor’s roster before changing spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the contractor for a straight answer about booked work instead of repeating a message from someone outside the site. AGI reaches the office tasks first, and robots are expected around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plans and records I handle as crew lead are thinking work, so AGI could do them by 2028. Robots follow in 2031, which means the carpentry itself is exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working and keep my reserve intact. In 2029 I’d ask the contractor about the job list and contact nearby builders if my hours had been cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because two years is short and robots eventually reach my trade. The reserve lets me make calls and wait a little, but it doesn’t make the work secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a nearby builder be a safe answer if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn’t call it safe; I’d ask whether they had paid work now and treat it as a bridge. I would keep enough savings for rent rather than move on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expense would you change first if the next job were delayed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d pause replacing my old sofa and leave the savings for rent and food. It is not a large sacrifice, but keeping a reserve is more useful than buying something new while hours are uncertain.

say: I’d ask the contractor about **booked work**, not repeat outside rumors.
I’d note that robots are expected around **2031**.
think: I expect AGI could take plans and records in **my lead role** by 2028.
I know the robots expose **carpentry itself** later.
do: Keep leading my current **crew** while work remains.
Leave my **reserve** intact for a contract gap.
Contact **nearby builders** if hours are cut in 2029.
feel: I feel **anxious** because two years is short and robots reach my trade later.
S2.quote: I wouldn’t call it safe; I’d ask whether they had paid work now and treat it as a bridge.
fieldNote: Chloe describes an application as **temporary income**, not protection.
Her reserve offers time to check actual work, but cannot secure **future carpentry wages** or guarantee a new position.

steps.text: Keep leading my current crew while work remains
Leave my reserve available for a contract gap
Contact nearby builders if hours are cut in 2029
Pause replacing the old sofa if the next job is delayed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives a company time to train crews and explain changes before the roster gets changed. I want the information to come from someone who can answer questions about our site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take the planning side in 2031, and the hands-on work faces robots around 2034. I have more time than in the fast case, but I can’t assume the same job continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get the foreman to show me the system on the site and keep notes of how it changes the work. In 2032 I’d check my hours and contact another builder if the contractor had reduced my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the end point, but five years gives me a chance to build savings and prepare. I’d rather take one useful step at a time than rush into a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time let you do that the two-year warning does not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have more months to add to my reserve and see whether the system is useful. I’d try a short training session before paying for anything longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would construction office scheduling be a protected job after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn’t count on that; scheduling is thinking work too. I’d learn what I need for this role and ask builders about actual openings as the dates approach.

say: I’d ask a manager to explain changes before the **roster shifts**.
I want site crews to hear **consistent information**.
think: I expect AGI could take planning by **2031**.
I can prepare, but I can’t assume the **same job continues**.
do: Ask the foreman to show me the system on **site**.
Contact another builder if **shifts are reduced**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but the longer lead time helps me prepare.
S3.quote: I’d try a short training session before paying for anything longer.
fieldNote: Chloe chooses **small trials** before committing money to training, and checks whether lessons apply to current work.
She knows planning is exposed too and checks actual **local openings**.

steps.text: Learn the new system beside the foreman on site
Add to my reserve through the additional warning years
Contact another builder if shifts fall after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is time to prepare, but it isn’t a promise that the job lasts. I’d want the contractor to offer training tied to actual site work, not just a certificate to hang on a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save more and learn the tools over ten years. AGI still reaches planning in 2036 and robots reach carpentry in 2039, so I don’t think an office job is protected either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and take practical training if the contractor offers it. In 2037 I’d review my hours, savings and local openings, and call other builders if the work had slowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me a useful runway, although I’m uneasy about the later robot date. I can save steadily and make choices with evidence, but I don’t know which jobs will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to decide before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d decide whether to stay in this town or move closer to more building work. I’d visit first and talk with employers before giving up my flat or spending the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a long course during the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d consider one only if employers can point to a job that needs it. I wouldn’t borrow heavily for office scheduling when AGI is meant to do that kind of thinking work.

say: I’d use the decade to **prepare**, not assume the job lasts.
I want training tied to **real site work**.
think: I could save and learn tools over **ten years**.
I don’t think office work or carpentry is **protected** after the dates.
do: Keep leading carpentry work while current **contracts last**.
Review my hours and savings in **2037**.
Call other **builders** if local work slows.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the later robot date, with time to plan.
S4.quote: I’d want the contractor to offer training tied to actual site work, not just a certificate to hang on a wall.
fieldNote: Chloe wants **job-linked training** and avoids borrowing for a vague promise from a school or recruiter.
She would consider moving only after checking **employer demand** and living costs.

steps.text: Keep leading carpentry work while current contracts last
Take practical training offered by the contractor
Visit busier areas before deciding whether to move

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years is a short time before thinking work changes and robots follow. I’d want practical training during paid time and clear information about the contractor’s booked work so I can plan my reserve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask who checks whether training leads to a real job. A certificate is only useful if a builder needs that skill, and I’d want to know before spending my savings.

headlineQuote: A certificate is only useful if a builder needs that skill, and I’d want to know before spending my savings.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old crew lead** who learned carpentry in her aunt’s joinery shop.
She lives alone, earns typical pay, and has **a few months saved**.
She will adopt proven tools but wants **practical demonstrations** and job-linked training.
Some local employers and her reserve give her options, while robots eventually expose **her trade**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries Chloe most because there is little time before planning changes and robots follow.
whatWouldHelp: Practical **paid training** and clear information about booked work would help Chloe plan her reserve.
